pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l01.q: What produces platelets, and how long do they normally live?
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l01.why: Platelets are fragments shed from megakaryocytes in the marrow, with a lifespan of 8-10 days and a normal count of 150,000-400,000/microliter. Erythrocytes live about 120 days, most white cells survive far shorter, and hepatocytes are liver cells, not platelet precursors.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l01.q: Which plasma protein maintains oncotic pressure and keeps fluid inside the vessels?
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l01.why: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and holds fluid inside vessels by oncotic pressure; low albumin lets fluid leak into tissue as edema. Fibrinogen builds clots, globulins include antibodies, and thrombopoietin is a hormone, not a structural plasma protein.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l02.q: Which lab pattern points to hemolysis rather than underproduction as the cause of anemia?
choices: Low reticulocyte count with normal bilirubin
High reticulocyte count, high indirect bilirubin, high LDH, low haptoglobin
High reticulocyte count with high haptoglobin
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l02.why: Hemolysis is destruction, so the marrow responds with more reticulocytes while breakdown products (indirect bilirubin, LDH) rise and haptoglobin, which mops up free hemoglobin, is consumed and falls. Underproduction instead shows a low reticulocyte count.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l02.q: What triggers a vaso-occlusive crisis in sickle cell disease?
choices: Hypoxia, dehydration, infection, cold or acidosis
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l02.why: Anything that lowers oxygen tension or concentrates the blood promotes hemoglobin S polymerization: hypoxia, dehydration, infection, cold, acidosis and stress. High oxygen and hydration are protective, not provocative.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l03.q: What is the purpose of a crossmatch beyond a type and screen?
choices: It physically mixes patient plasma with the specific donor unit to prove compatibility
It replaces the need for a type and screen
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l03.why: Type and screen identifies ABO/Rh and screens for unexpected antibodies; crossmatch goes further by physically testing the patient's plasma against the actual unit to be transfused, adding about 15-30 minutes of extra safety.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l03.q: Which blood product specifically corrects a low fibrinogen or replaces von Willebrand factor and factor VIII?
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l03.why: Cryoprecipitate is concentrated fibrinogen, factor VIII and von Willebrand factor, used when fibrinogen falls under 150 mg/dL or in DIC. Fresh frozen plasma carries all factors but in a larger, less concentrated volume.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l04.q: What is the role of von Willebrand factor in primary hemostasis?
choices: It acts as the glue that lets platelets adhere to exposed collagen
It is a vitamin K dependent clotting factor
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l04.why: Von Willebrand factor bridges platelets to exposed subendothelial collagen after vessel injury, enabling the platelet plug of primary hemostasis. Fibrin formation belongs to secondary hemostasis, and plasmin, not von Willebrand factor, dissolves clots.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l04.q: What does a rising D-dimer indicate, and why is it not diagnostic on its own?
choices: That clot has formed and been broken down somewhere, but it is sensitive and not specific
A diagnosis of DIC by itself
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l04.why: D-dimer is a fibrin breakdown fragment, so a rise means clot formation and fibrinolysis occurred somewhere, but it can rise for many reasons, so it is used to rule out rather than to rule in a specific diagnosis.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l05.q: Why is Homans sign (calf pain on dorsiflexion) not used to diagnose DVT?
choices: It is unreliable and should not change clinical decision-making
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l05.why: Homans sign has poor sensitivity and specificity, so relying on it risks both missing true clots and chasing false positives; structured scoring plus D-dimer or ultrasound is the actual pathway.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l05.q: What does dead space physiology explain about the effect of a pulmonary embolism on gas exchange?
choices: The lung segment is perfused but not ventilated
The lung segment is ventilated but not perfused, so gas exchange fails there
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l05.why: A clot obstructs blood flow to a segment that is still receiving air, so that segment is ventilated but unperfused (dead space) and cannot exchange gas, which is why hypoxia and tachypnea appear even with clear lungs on exam.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l06.q: What are the three mechanical/chemical steps that produce the five signs of inflammation?
choices: Vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, and chemotaxis
Antibody production, memory formation, and class switching
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l06.why: Vasodilation causes redness and heat, increased capillary permeability causes swelling and pain, and chemotaxis draws neutrophils then macrophages to the site — together producing rubor, calor, tumor, dolor and loss of function.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l06.q: Which immunoglobulin class is the only one that crosses the placenta?
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l06.why: IgG is small enough to cross the placenta and provides passive protection to the newborn for the first months of life. IgM is too large, IgA protects mucous membranes, and IgE drives allergic responses.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l07.q: At what CD4 count is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis typically started?
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l07.why: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia risk rises sharply once CD4 falls under 200 cells/microliter, which is the threshold for starting prophylaxis, typically trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, rather than waiting for a first infection.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l07.q: Why can a patient on chronic steroids have a perforated bowel with a benign-appearing abdominal exam?
choices: Steroids suppress the inflammatory response that normally produces guarding, rebound and fever
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l07.why: Chronic steroids blunt the inflammatory signs that would normally alert a clinician to a surgical abdomen, so a benign exam does not rule out a catastrophic problem in this population.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l08.q: Which organism is the leading cause of both community-acquired pneumonia and bacterial meningitis in adults, and why does it especially threaten asplenic patients?
choices: Escherichia coli, because it is gram-negative
Streptococcus pneumoniae, because it is an encapsulated organism the spleen normally clears
Pseudomonas aeruginosa, because it thrives on wet surfaces
Clostridioides difficile, because it forms spores
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l08.why: Streptococcus pneumoniae is encapsulated, and the spleen is a key site for clearing encapsulated organisms, so patients without a working spleen are at extreme risk from it specifically.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l08.q: What distinguishes colonization from infection, and why does the distinction matter for treatment?
choices: Colonization is presence without tissue damage or host response, and treating it usually causes harm rather than benefit
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l08.why: A colonized patient harbors the organism without illness; treating that colonization exposes the patient to antibiotic side effects and resistance selection without benefit, unlike treating true infection.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l09.q: Which wound healing phase is responsible for collagen deposition and new capillary growth?
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l09.why: During proliferation, roughly days 4-21, fibroblasts lay down collagen, angiogenesis brings in new capillaries, and epithelium migrates across the wound surface. Hemostasis is the initial clotting response, inflammation clears debris, and remodeling reorganizes collagen over months to years.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l09.q: What is the maximum tensile strength scar tissue ever reaches compared to uninjured skin?
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l09.why: Even after full remodeling over one to two years, scar tissue reaches only about 80% of the original tensile strength, which is why healed wounds remain a point of relative weakness.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l10.q: Which hormone triggers ovulation, and what causes its release?
choices: LH; triggered by a surge in estrogen from the maturing follicle
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l10.why: Rising estrogen from the maturing follicle triggers a surge in luteinizing hormone (LH), which causes the follicle to release the egg around day 14. hCG comes later, only if implantation occurs.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l10.q: Why does RhoGAM matter for an Rh-negative mother, and when is it given?
choices: It treats an active Rh reaction; given only after birth
It prevents sensitization against Rh-positive fetal blood; given around 28 weeks and after delivery, miscarriage, trauma or bleeding
It is given only to Rh-positive mothers
It replaces the need for prenatal care
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l10.why: An Rh-negative mother exposed to Rh-positive fetal blood can form anti-D antibodies that attack a future Rh-positive pregnancy; RhoGAM is given proactively to prevent that sensitization from ever occurring.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l11.q: Which two tests distinguish B12 deficiency from folate deficiency when both cause macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils?
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l11.why: Both B12 and folate deficiency are megaloblastic and raise homocysteine, but methylmalonic acid is elevated only in B12 deficiency, which matters because B12 deficiency also causes neurologic damage that folate replacement alone will not stop.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l11.q: In a stable, non-bleeding patient without acute coronary syndrome, what hemoglobin threshold typically triggers transfusion?
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l11.why: The standard restrictive transfusion threshold in a stable patient is a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL (8 g/dL with acute coronary syndrome), because symptoms and the rate of the drop matter more than chasing a higher number in someone stable.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l12.q: Why does desmopressin help in mild hemophilia A but not hemophilia B?
choices: It releases stored factor VIII, and hemophilia B is a factor IX deficiency that desmopressin does not affect
It works by increasing platelet count
It is only used in von Willebrand disease
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l12.why: Desmopressin triggers release of stored factor VIII (and von Willebrand factor) from endothelial cells, which helps mild hemophilia A, but hemophilia B is a deficiency of factor IX, a different molecule entirely.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l12.q: What defines heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and what must never be given?
choices: A slow platelet rise over weeks; give more heparin
A platelet fall of more than 50% at day 5-10 of heparin with a tendency to clot; platelets must not be given
An isolated low white count; give steroids
A normal platelet count with bleeding; give plasma
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l12.why: HIT is an immune reaction that paradoxically promotes clotting despite a falling platelet count, typically 5-10 days into heparin exposure; platelet transfusion can worsen thrombosis, so a non-heparin anticoagulant is started instead.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l13.q: Why is tranexamic acid only beneficial when given within 3 hours of injury or delivery?
choices: Trials showed benefit only within that early window; given later it does not show the same benefit
It requires refrigeration that expires at 3 hours
It only works in postpartum hemorrhage, not trauma
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l13.why: Evidence from major trauma and postpartum hemorrhage trials showed a mortality benefit from tranexamic acid only when given within about 3 hours of the bleeding event; delayed administration does not show the same benefit.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l13.q: What options exist for a patient who declines whole blood but may still accept some blood-derived products?
choices: No alternatives exist once a patient refuses transfusion
Albumin, clotting factor concentrates, PCC, cryoprecipitate or cell salvage, decided component by component
The refusal is automatically overridden in an emergency
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l13.why: A patient's refusal of blood is not necessarily all-or-nothing; many patients accept specific components such as albumin, factor concentrates, PCC, cryoprecipitate or intraoperative cell salvage, so each is discussed individually.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l14.q: What does 'undetectable equals untransmittable' mean clinically?
choices: A patient with undetectable viral load can still transmit HIV sexually at the same rate
A patient on effective antiretroviral therapy with a sustained undetectable viral load does not sexually transmit HIV
It applies only to needlestick exposures
It means the patient is cured
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l14.why: Sustained viral suppression on effective antiretroviral therapy eliminates sexual transmission risk, a finding that reshaped counseling and public health messaging, though it does not mean the virus is eradicated.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l14.q: Which needlestick exposure carries the highest transmission risk per exposure: HIV, hepatitis C, or hepatitis B in an unvaccinated worker?
choices: Hepatitis B, up to about 30% in an unvaccinated worker
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l14.why: Per hollow-bore needlestick from an infected source, hepatitis B carries the highest risk in an unvaccinated worker (up to about 30%), compared with roughly 1.8% for hepatitis C and about 0.3% for HIV.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l15.q: Which antibodies are specific for systemic lupus erythematosus, as opposed to ANA which is sensitive but non-specific?
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l15.why: Anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith antibodies are relatively specific for lupus and, combined with falling complement levels, can indicate an active flare. The other antibody pairs belong to different rheumatologic diseases.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l15.q: What long-standing complication of rheumatoid arthritis creates danger during intubation or neck manipulation?
choices: Atlantoaxial instability from cervical spine erosion
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l15.why: Chronic rheumatoid arthritis can erode the ligaments stabilizing the atlantoaxial joint, creating instability that risks spinal cord injury during neck extension for intubation or other manipulation.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l16.q: What is the difference between cancer stage and grade?
choices: Stage describes cell appearance, grade describes spread
Stage describes how far the cancer has spread using TNM; grade describes how abnormal the cells look under the microscope
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l16.why: Stage answers how far the disease has spread and drives prognosis and treatment planning, while grade is a separate histologic assessment of how abnormal, or differentiated, the tumor cells appear.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l16.q: Why should calcium not be reflexively replaced in tumor lysis syndrome despite a low serum calcium?
choices: Calcium replacement is always safe and recommended
With phosphate very high, giving calcium risks calcium-phosphate precipitation in tissues
Low calcium is never seen in tumor lysis syndrome
Calcium replacement treats the underlying cause
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l16.why: Tumor lysis syndrome drives phosphate very high; adding calcium in that setting risks calcium phosphate crystal precipitation in the kidneys and other tissues, so correction focuses on hydration and uric acid reduction.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l17.q: Which sign indicates the skin is failing as an organ and belongs to TEN, pemphigus vulgaris, or staph scalded skin syndrome?
choices: A positive Nikolsky sign, where gentle lateral pressure shears the top skin layer away
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l17.why: A positive Nikolsky sign reflects loss of cohesion between skin layers and marks conditions where the skin is failing as a barrier organ, requiring burn-unit level care.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l17.q: What primary lesion terminology describes a broad, raised, flat-topped area of skin?
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l17.why: A plaque is a broad raised area, as opposed to a small papule, while a macule is flat and a vesicle is a small fluid-filled lesion — this vocabulary is the starting point for describing any rash precisely.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l18.q: Why is thiamine given before dextrose-containing fluids in a patient with prolonged hyperemesis gravidarum?
choices: A glucose load in a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l18.why: Prolonged vomiting can deplete thiamine stores, and giving glucose before replacing thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy, so thiamine is given first as a simple, low-risk precaution.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l18.q: Which four causes make up the 'four Ts' of postpartum hemorrhage, and which is most common?
choices: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin — with Tone (uterine atony) causing 70-80% of cases
Toxin, Trauma, Tissue, Time — with Toxin most common
Tone, Temperature, Tissue, Thrombin — with Temperature most common
Trauma is the most common cause at over 90%
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l18.why: The four Ts organize the differential for postpartum hemorrhage, and uterine atony accounts for 70-80% of cases — which is why fundal massage and uterotonics are the first response.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l19.q: What is the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, and why is it not treated as a drug allergy?
choices: An allergic reaction to penicillin requiring epinephrine
Fever, chills and worsening rash within 24 hours of treating syphilis, caused by dying organisms
A sign of treatment failure requiring a second antibiotic
A permanent complication of syphilis treatment
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l19.why: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction follows successful antibiotic killing of spirochetes and the resulting release of their contents, producing transient fever and rash; it does not mean the patient is allergic or that treatment failed.

pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l19.q: Why is manual detorsion of a twisted testicle considered a temporizing measure rather than definitive treatment?
choices: It may relieve ischemia temporarily while awaiting surgery, but does not replace operative fixation
It is performed instead of imaging in all cases
pa-anatomy-heme-immune-repro-l19.why: Manual detorsion can restore some blood flow while imaging or the operating room is arranged, but it is not a substitute for surgical exploration and fixation, since recurrence or incomplete detorsion is common.

quiz.q: A patient's differential shows neutrophils 40%, lymphocytes 52%, with a total white count of 6,800/microliter and three days of fever, cough and myalgias. Which process best fits?
quiz.why: Lymphocyte predominance points toward a viral process rather than bacterial infection, which classically raises neutrophils. Acute leukemia typically shows blasts and very abnormal counts, and parasites raise eosinophils, not lymphocytes.

quiz.q: Where does adult hematopoiesis normally occur?
choices: Red marrow of the pelvis, sternum, ribs, vertebrae and long bone ends
Yellow marrow of the long bone shafts
quiz.why: In adults, active red marrow is concentrated in the pelvis, sternum, ribs, vertebrae and proximal long bones; the shafts of long bones convert to fatty yellow marrow. Liver and spleen are fetal sites that resume hematopoiesis only in disease.

quiz.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease has a stable hemoglobin of 9.4 g/dL and no symptoms. What best explains this baseline?
choices: Undiagnosed iron deficiency requiring urgent workup
Reduced erythropoietin production by the failing kidneys
quiz.why: The kidney makes erythropoietin, so chronic kidney disease blunts red cell production and a hemoglobin around 9-10 g/dL becomes the patient's expected baseline. It is not automatically a bleed or a vitamin deficiency.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old with sickle cell disease is functionally asplenic from childhood infarction. Which vaccination priority follows from this?
choices: Vaccination against encapsulated organisms such as pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b
quiz.why: Functional asplenia removes the main defense against encapsulated bacteria, so pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination are prioritized and any fever is treated as possible sepsis.

quiz.q: A patient with known alcohol use disorder has an MCV of 108 fL and a mildly elevated homocysteine with a normal methylmalonic acid. Which mechanism best fits?
choices: Folate deficiency and direct marrow toxicity from alcohol
quiz.why: A normal methylmalonic acid argues against B12 deficiency, while alcohol both impairs folate and directly suppresses the marrow, producing macrocytosis independent of B12 status. Iron deficiency causes microcytosis, not macrocytosis.

quiz.q: Which physical exam location is most reliable for detecting pallor from anemia?
choices: Conjunctiva, palmar creases and nail beds
quiz.why: The conjunctiva, palmar creases and nail beds are more reliable than facial or forehead skin, where pigmentation and lighting make pallor hard to judge.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a crossmatch beyond a type and screen for a scheduled, non-emergent transfusion?
choices: It replaces the need for a type and screen
It physically mixes patient plasma with the specific donor unit to prove compatibility before it is given
quiz.why: Type and screen identifies ABO/Rh and screens for unexpected antibodies; crossmatch goes further by physically testing plasma against the actual unit, adding about 15-30 minutes of extra safety.

quiz.q: A trauma patient in extremis needs blood before a type and screen result is available. What is given?
choices: No blood until typing is complete
Uncrossmatched O negative, or O positive in men and older women, given immediately
quiz.why: Emergency release provides uncrossmatched O red cells within seconds for a patient who cannot wait the 30-45 minutes a type and screen takes. Withholding blood for typing in an exsanguinating patient causes preventable death.

quiz.q: During a massive transfusion, which electrolyte should be actively monitored because stored blood's anticoagulant binds it?
quiz.why: Stored blood is anticoagulated with citrate, which chelates ionized calcium; rapid transfusion can cause hypocalcemia that worsens both coagulopathy and cardiac contractility.

quiz.q: Which platelet count carries the highest risk of spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage?
quiz.why: Below 10,000/microliter the risk of spontaneous bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage, rises sharply, which is the usual transfusion threshold in a stable patient.

quiz.q: A patient takes aspirin daily and needs emergency surgery in 2 hours after a fall. Why can platelet transfusion help restore function faster than waiting for aspirin to wear off?
choices: Aspirin's effect reverses spontaneously within hours
Aspirin irreversibly blocks cyclooxygenase in existing platelets for their whole 8-10 day life, so only new, unblocked platelets restore function quickly
Platelet transfusion has no role in antiplatelet reversal
quiz.why: Because platelets have no nucleus, once aspirin acetylates their cyclooxygenase enzyme that platelet is impaired for its whole lifespan; only transfusing fresh, unaffected platelets restores function quickly.

quiz.q: Which two coagulation tests converge to reflect the common pathway, ending in thrombin generation?
quiz.why: The extrinsic pathway (PT/INR) and intrinsic pathway (PTT) both feed into the common pathway at factor X, generating thrombin and fibrin. D-dimer measures breakdown, not generation.

quiz.q: A patient with a low pretest probability Wells score for DVT has a negative D-dimer. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: DVT is effectively excluded without further imaging
quiz.why: A low clinical probability combined with a negative D-dimer has a very low likelihood of missed DVT and effectively rules it out, avoiding unnecessary imaging.

quiz.q: Why is the classic ECG finding S1Q3T3 an unreliable way to diagnose pulmonary embolism?
choices: It appears in the majority of PE cases and is highly specific
It appears only in a minority of PE cases; sinus tachycardia is the far more common ECG finding
It is only seen in DVT, not PE
ECG cannot show any abnormality in PE
quiz.why: Most patients with PE simply show sinus tachycardia; the S1Q3T3 pattern of right heart strain is classic to teach but appears in only a minority of cases, so its absence does not exclude PE.

quiz.q: Which measure is the most effective way to prevent DVT in a hospitalized, immobile patient?
choices: Early ambulation, sequential compression devices and prophylactic anticoagulation
Elevating the legs without any other measure
quiz.why: Prevention targets Virchow's triad directly: moving the patient reduces stasis, mechanical compression augments venous return, and prophylactic anticoagulation reduces hypercoagulability.

quiz.q: Which cells mature in the thymus and directly kill virus-infected cells?
quiz.why: T cells mature in the thymus; cytotoxic CD8 T cells kill virus-infected and tumor cells directly. B cells mature in bone marrow and make antibodies rather than killing cells directly.

quiz.q: A patient develops hives and mild wheezing within minutes of eating shellfish. Which hypersensitivity mechanism is responsible?
choices: Type I, IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation releasing histamine
Type II, antibody against self cells
Type IV, delayed T cell response
quiz.why: An immediate reaction within minutes, driven by IgE bound to mast cells releasing histamine, is the definition of type I hypersensitivity, the same mechanism behind anaphylaxis.

quiz.q: A patient with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis develops edema and hematuria two weeks after a strep throat infection. Which hypersensitivity type explains the kidney injury?
choices: Type III, immune complexes depositing in the glomeruli
quiz.why: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type III reaction: antigen-antibody complexes deposit in the glomerular basement membrane and trigger inflammation over days to weeks.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old with septic shock has a temperature of 35.0 C rather than fever. How should this be interpreted?
choices: A reassuring sign that infection is resolving
An ominous sign reflecting a failing physiologic response, associated with higher mortality than fever
quiz.why: Hypothermia in sepsis reflects an inadequate or overwhelmed host response and is associated with worse outcomes than a febrile response.

quiz.q: A transplant recipient on lifelong immunosuppression presents with vague malaise and low-grade fever. Why is rejection difficult to distinguish from infection here?
choices: Rejection only affects lab values, never symptoms
Both rejection and infection can present with similar nonspecific systemic symptoms in an immunosuppressed host
quiz.why: Immunosuppression blunts the specific signs that would normally separate one process from another, so transplant rejection and infection can look alike clinically and require targeted testing.

quiz.q: A neutropenic patient's chest radiograph is read as normal despite a strong clinical suspicion for pneumonia. What is the best explanation?
choices: Radiographic infiltrates are largely formed by neutrophils, which this patient lacks, so the film can lag behind the disease
The patient does not have pneumonia
Radiographs cannot detect any lung pathology
quiz.why: The visible infiltrate on a chest film is inflammatory exudate built mostly by neutrophils; without enough of them the radiographic evidence simply may not have formed yet.

quiz.q: Which stain characteristic explains why gram-negative bacteria appear pink rather than purple?
choices: A thick peptidoglycan wall traps the dye
A thin wall with an outer lipid membrane releases the crystal violet dye, taking the pink counterstain instead
They lack a cell wall entirely
They are resistant to all stains
quiz.why: Gram-negative organisms have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer lipid membrane; the decolorizing step washes out the crystal violet, so they take up the pink counterstain.

quiz.q: A hospitalized patient develops a new ventilator-associated pneumonia caused by an organism that thrives on wet surfaces and is intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics. Which organism fits best?
quiz.why: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is classically associated with wet hospital environments, ventilators and burns, and carries intrinsic resistance to many antibiotic classes.

quiz.q: Antibiotic stewardship principles include which of the following?
choices: Always choosing the broadest-spectrum agent available
Continuing broad-spectrum antibiotics indefinitely to be safe
Choosing the narrowest effective spectrum, correct dose, and shortest effective duration, then de-escalating once cultures return
quiz.why: Stewardship balances effective treatment against the pressure every exposure puts on resistance: narrow the spectrum as soon as culture data allow, dose correctly, and stop as soon as safe.

quiz.q: Which wound closure method is chosen when a heavily contaminated wound is left open initially, then closed after several days once infection risk has been controlled?
quiz.why: Tertiary intention deliberately delays closure until contamination is controlled, combining some of the speed of primary closure with the safety of allowing drainage first.

quiz.q: Which factor delays wound healing?
quiz.why: Diabetes impairs perfusion and immune function, and smoking causes vasoconstriction and reduces oxygen delivery, both slowing healing. The other options all support healing.

quiz.q: A patient's chest has non-blanching purpuric spots, fever and looks acutely ill. What should be suspected first?
quiz.why: A non-blanching rash with fever and toxic appearance signals blood outside the vessels from a disseminated infection and is treated as meningococcemia until ruled out.

quiz.q: Where does fertilization normally occur?
quiz.why: The egg is released from the ovary and normally meets sperm in the fallopian tube, where fertilization occurs before the embryo travels to the uterus to implant.

quiz.q: A pregnant patient's hemoglobin drops from a pre-pregnancy 13.5 g/dL to 11.2 g/dL by the third trimester with no symptoms and normal iron studies. What best explains this?
choices: Physiologic dilution from a plasma volume increase that outpaces red cell mass expansion
quiz.why: Plasma volume rises about 40-50% in pregnancy while red cell mass increases less, producing an expected physiologic dilutional drop in hemoglobin, especially with normal iron studies.

quiz.q: A 32-year-old at 26 weeks develops a blood pressure of 148/94 with new proteinuria and a headache. What is this?
quiz.why: New hypertension of 140/90 or higher after 20 weeks with proteinuria or end-organ signs such as headache defines preeclampsia.

quiz.q: A patient has anemia with a low reticulocyte production index. What does this indicate about the mechanism?
choices: The marrow is compensating appropriately for destruction
The marrow is underproducing red cells
The patient is bleeding acutely and compensating well
quiz.why: A low reticulocyte response means the marrow is not mounting an adequate production response, pointing toward underproduction rather than a process of ongoing loss or destruction.

quiz.q: Which finding on a peripheral smear suggests hereditary spherocytosis or warm autoimmune hemolysis?
quiz.why: Spherocytes, red cells that have lost their normal biconcave shape, point to hereditary spherocytosis or warm autoimmune hemolysis. Schistocytes suggest mechanical fragmentation and bite cells suggest G6PD deficiency.

quiz.q: A patient has anemia, thrombocytopenia, and schistocytes on smear, but a normal PT and PTT. Why does the normal coagulation panel matter diagnostically?
choices: It argues against DIC and points toward a microangiopathy like TTP or HUS instead, where the coagulation cascade itself is not consumed
quiz.why: DIC consumes clotting factors and prolongs PT and PTT, while TTP and HUS are primarily platelet-consuming microangiopathies that leave the coagulation cascade intact.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old has petechiae and bruising two weeks after a viral illness, with an isolated platelet count of 15,000/microliter and an otherwise normal exam. What is the expected course?
choices: Often self-limited in children, frequently resolving on its own
quiz.why: Pediatric ITP commonly follows a viral illness and often resolves spontaneously within weeks to months, unlike the more often chronic course seen in adults.

quiz.q: Which combination of findings distinguishes von Willebrand disease from hemophilia in presentation?
choices: Von Willebrand disease causes deep joint bleeds like hemophilia
Hemophilia affects women equally to men
Von Willebrand disease commonly causes mucocutaneous bleeding such as heavy menstrual periods and affects men and women equally, unlike X-linked hemophilia
Von Willebrand disease is always more severe than hemophilia
quiz.why: Von Willebrand disease is autosomal and affects both sexes, often presenting as lifelong heavy menstrual bleeding, while hemophilia is X-linked recessive and almost exclusively affects males.

quiz.q: A patient in DIC needs an invasive procedure. Platelets are 38,000/microliter and fibrinogen is 80 mg/dL, without active bleeding currently. What is appropriate?
choices: No product replacement is ever given in DIC
Replace platelets and give cryoprecipitate before the procedure since correction is needed for the intervention
quiz.why: In DIC, product replacement is reserved for active bleeding or before a procedure; correcting a low platelet count and low fibrinogen beforehand reduces procedural bleeding risk.

quiz.q: Which of the four elements of the 'lethal diamond' in massive transfusion is specifically caused by citrate in stored blood?
quiz.why: Citrate is the anticoagulant used to store blood, and it binds ionized calcium; rapid transfusion can drop calcium enough to worsen clotting and cardiac function.

quiz.q: Which transfusion reaction may be cautiously restarted after treatment if only mild hives occur and then resolve?
choices: Mild allergic reaction with hives only
quiz.why: A mild allergic reaction limited to hives, once treated with an antihistamine and resolved, is the one reaction where the same transfusion may cautiously continue.

quiz.q: A postpartum hemorrhage patient receives tranexamic acid 4 hours after delivery. What should be expected?
choices: Full benefit, since the window is 6 hours
Reduced or absent benefit, because the effective window for mortality reduction is within about 3 hours of delivery
It works better the later it is given
quiz.why: Tranexamic acid's mortality benefit in postpartum hemorrhage is established for administration within roughly 3 hours; giving it later is less likely to provide the same benefit.

quiz.q: A patient starts effective antiretroviral therapy for a CD4 count of 30 and, within 2 weeks, develops worsening symptoms from a previously silent infection as their CD4 count rises. What is this?
choices: A new opportunistic infection unrelated to treatment
Drug allergy to the antiretroviral regimen
quiz.why: As a severely suppressed immune system recovers, it can mount an exaggerated inflammatory response against a previously subclinical infection, making the patient appear to worsen while actually improving.

quiz.q: Which vaccine requires two doses starting at age 50 (or younger if immunocompromised)?
quiz.why: The recombinant zoster vaccine is given in a 2-dose series starting at age 50, or from age 19 in immunocompromised patients, to prevent shingles.

quiz.q: A patient sustains a dirty, contaminated wound and last received a tetanus booster 6 years ago with a complete childhood series. What is indicated?
choices: No booster needed since it has been under 10 years
A tetanus booster now, since dirty wounds need one after 5 years
Tetanus immune globulin only, no vaccine
Nothing is needed regardless of wound type
quiz.why: A dirty or contaminated wound needs a booster if the last dose was more than 5 years ago, compared with the 10-year threshold for a clean minor wound.

quiz.q: A patient with known systemic lupus erythematosus develops a new drop in complement levels and a rising anti-double-stranded DNA titer. What does this suggest?
choices: A drug-induced lupus reaction that will resolve on its own
quiz.why: Falling complement with rising anti-dsDNA is a recognized pattern of an active lupus flare, reflecting immune complex formation and consumption of complement.

quiz.q: Which joint pattern is most consistent with osteoarthritis rather than rheumatoid arthritis?
choices: Morning stiffness lasting over an hour that improves with use
quiz.why: Osteoarthritis characteristically involves the distal interphalangeal joints, which rheumatoid arthritis classically spares in favor of symmetric MCP and wrist involvement.

quiz.q: A patient with longstanding systemic sclerosis develops a sudden severe rise in blood pressure with acute kidney injury. What is the specific first-line treatment?
quiz.why: Scleroderma renal crisis is treated specifically with an ACE inhibitor, which is unusual since ACE inhibitors are typically avoided in acute kidney injury, but here they address the renin-driven pathophysiology.

quiz.q: Which cancer treatment's side effects are managed with corticosteroids rather than antibiotics, because the mechanism is autoimmune?
choices: Checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy toxicity such as colitis or pneumonitis
quiz.why: Checkpoint inhibitors release the brakes on T cells, so their toxicities are autoimmune in nature and are treated with immunosuppression, typically corticosteroids, not antimicrobials.

quiz.q: Which cancer causes the most cancer deaths overall, despite not being the single most commonly diagnosed?
quiz.why: Lung cancer leads cancer mortality by a wide margin because it is often diagnosed at a late, less treatable stage, even though breast and prostate cancers are diagnosed more frequently.

quiz.q: A patient with lymphoma develops facial and arm swelling with distended neck veins that worsens when lying flat. What is the true emergency to watch for in this presentation, as opposed to the swelling itself?
quiz.why: This is superior vena cava syndrome; the genuine emergency is airway compromise or cerebral edema, which requires urgent recognition beyond the visible swelling.

quiz.q: Which finding is one of the five 'red flag' features that should prompt escalation for any rash?
choices: A rash that blanches with pressure
A rash present for years unchanged
quiz.why: Mucous membrane involvement is one of the recognized red flags, alongside non-blanching with fever, painful skin, sloughing skin, and rapid spread over hours.

quiz.q: A patient develops dozens of tiny sterile pustules on red skin just 2 days after starting a new antibiotic. Which drug eruption is this?
quiz.why: AGEP has the fastest onset of the drug eruptions, typically 1-3 days, presenting as numerous small sterile pustules on erythematous skin.

quiz.q: Which feature of a pigmented skin lesion is most concerning for melanoma under the ABCDE criteria?
choices: A diameter under 3 mm that has been stable for years
Irregular borders, color variation and recent evolution in size or shape
A lesion identical to the patient's other moles
quiz.why: ABCDE criteria flag asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter over 6 mm and evolution as melanoma warning signs.

quiz.q: A patient at 28 weeks undergoes a 50 g glucose challenge test that returns abnormal. What is the next step?
choices: Diagnose gestational diabetes immediately and start insulin
Repeat the 50 g test in one month
Proceed to a 100 g three-hour glucose tolerance test to confirm the diagnosis
quiz.why: The 50 g glucose challenge is a screening test; an abnormal result is followed by the more definitive 100 g three-hour tolerance test before diagnosing gestational diabetes.

quiz.q: A patient receiving a magnesium sulfate infusion for preeclampsia with severe features loses her deep tendon reflexes. What is the correct next step?
choices: Stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate
Continue unchanged and recheck reflexes in 4 hours
Switch to an oral magnesium formulation
quiz.why: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the first clinical sign of magnesium toxicity; the infusion is stopped and calcium gluconate is given as the specific antidote.

quiz.q: A woman at 33 weeks has painful vaginal bleeding, a rigid tender uterus, and signs of fetal distress. What is this most consistent with?
quiz.why: Painful bleeding with a rigid, tender uterus and fetal distress is the classic picture of placental abruption, which can also trigger DIC. Previa and vasa previa cause painless bleeding.

quiz.q: Which contraceptive method has the lowest typical-use failure rate over one year?
choices: Long-acting reversible methods such as implants and IUDs
quiz.why: Implants and intrauterine devices have typical-use failure rates under 1% because they do not depend on user adherence, unlike pills, condoms and withdrawal.

quiz.q: A 40-year-old smoker requests hormonal contraception. Which class is contraindicated?
quiz.why: Estrogen-containing contraceptives are contraindicated in smokers age 35 or older because of increased thrombotic risk; progestin-only and non-hormonal options remain appropriate.

quiz.q: A patient has ischemic priapism lasting 6 hours in the setting of sickle cell disease. What is the appropriate initial management?
choices: Corporal aspiration and intracavernosal phenylephrine urgently
Observation, since it usually resolves on its own within 24 hours
quiz.why: Ischemic priapism is a compartment syndrome of the penis; beyond a few hours it risks permanent damage, so urgent aspiration and intracavernosal phenylephrine are standard emergency management.
